result: CryoET was used to obtain a 23.0 Å resolution structure of procentriole MT triplets from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, revealing that the A-tubule has 13 protofilaments in an elliptical arrangement while B- and C-tubules each have 10 protofilaments.
evaluation: Claims C1, C33-C39 collectively describe the experimental approach (cryoET), sample preparation (NFAp isolation), and structural findings (triplet resolution, protofilament composition). The resolution is reported with FSC curves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the structural features are consistent with prior observations cited in C38, providing convergent evidence for the triplet architecture.

result: Eleven non-tubulin microtubule inner proteins (MIPs) were identified associated with the triplet tubules through focused refinement, with seven MIPs localized at the inner junctions of A-B or B-C tubules, likely reinforcing the triplet structure.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C32, C48-C60 describe the identification and characterization of 11 MIPs using focused refinement (21.4-22.3 Å resolution). The structural details of individual MIPs (MIP1-MIP11) are documented with specific binding patterns, periodicities, and locations (Figure 2, Table 1). The inference that junction MIPs reinforce the triplet (C60) is reasonable given their crosslinking positions, though direct mechanical testing is not performed.

result: The pinhead structure connects the A-tubule to the cartwheel with 8 nm periodicity, consisting of pinbody (PinB) and two pinfeet (PinF1, PinF2) that bind to protofilament A3, with the high curvature at PFs A2-A3 potentially creating a unique anchoring site.
evaluation: Claims C40, C61-C69 describe the pinhead structure at 23.1 Å resolution (C61 cites consistency with Guichard et al., 2013; C64 cites agreement with Greenan et al., 2018). The 8 nm periodicity is documented, and structural features (PinB flexibility in C67, curvature at A2-A3 in C68) are observed. The inference about the anchoring site (C69) is speculative but reasonable given the structural observations.

result: The A-C linker forms a crisscross-shaped structure with five parts (central trunk, two arms, two legs) that bridges neighboring triplets, exhibiting structural heterogeneity and flexibility, with a doughnut-shaped density in Leg B having ~4 nm diameter and 8 nm periodicity.
evaluation: Claims C4, C41, C70-C81 describe the A-C linker structure obtained through extensive classification (4 and 6 classes in two schemes, Figure 3—figure supplements 1,4). The structural details (arms, legs, trunk composition) are documented at 23.1 Å resolution. The heterogeneity (C70, C73) is inferred from weaker density and multiple classes, which is a standard interpretation in cryoET. The doughnut-shaped density (C81) is clearly observed in the structure.

result: POC1 is inferred to be an integral component of the A-C linker, with its conserved WD40 β-propeller domain (predicted to have seven tandem repeats in Chlamydomonas) fitting into the ring density in Leg B and providing attachment sites for other A-C linker components.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C82-C92 propose POC1 as a component of the A-C linker based on: (1) localization studies showing POC1 at proximal ends (C82), (2) mutant phenotypes affecting A-C linker integrity (C85-C86), (3) predicted WD40 repeats (C87-C88), and (4) fitting of a WD40 crystal structure into the ring density (C89). However, the resolution (23.1 Å) is insufficient for definitive protein identification, no direct biochemical or genetic validation is provided, and C92 notes POC1 is also found at other locations. The inference is plausible but requires additional validation.

result: The A-C linker exhibits a twist motion with swing angles changing up to 10-16 degrees, resulting in progressive left-handed twisting of neighboring triplets along the procentriole and an iris diaphragm-like motion where the luminal diameter gradually increases from proximal to distal end.
evaluation: Claims C7, C93-C104 describe the twist motion based on classification analysis (4 and 6 classes) with quantified swing angles (Table 2, Figure 4). The central trunk as pivot point (C97) is clearly shown in overlays (Figure 4D,E). The iris diaphragm motion (C101) is documented in Video 5. Similar phenomena have been observed in other organisms (C102 cites multiple studies), and POC1 mutants show reduced twist angles (C103), providing independent support. The inference that this is a common feature (C104) is reasonable but extends beyond the data.

result: An assembly intermediate of the B-tubule was identified at both polar ends of the triplet, showing that B-tubule assembly initiates uni-directionally from PF B1 at the outer A-B junction with lateral expansion towards the luminal side, based on 157 subtomograms (88% from three major classes) showing incomplete B-tubules with strong densities for PFs B1-B3.
evaluation: Claims C8, C105-C117 describe the B-tubule intermediate based on classification of 2083 procentriole subtomograms, identifying 157 with partial B-tubules. The three major classes (88% of 157) show consistent structural features (strong B1-B3 densities). The length variation (C105, C110) and morphology (C107) support ongoing assembly. The uni-directional assembly mechanism (C117) is inferred from the consistent pattern across classes and is confirmed by direct visualization in tomograms (Figure 5D). The interpretation is consistent with prior EM studies cited in C152-C154.

result: An assembly intermediate of the C-tubule was identified showing bi-directional lateral assembly from both inner and outer B-C junctions, with 208 subtomograms (83% from three major classes) displaying PFs at both junctions with a gap between, and notably the A-C linker is visible even when the C-tubule is incomplete, indicating early establishment of inter-triplet linkage.
evaluation: Claims C118-C125 describe the C-tubule intermediate based on classification identifying 208 subtomograms with partial C-tubules. The three major classes (83% of 208) show consensus structure with PFs at both junctions (C121). The bi-directional assembly mechanism (C124) is inferred from the presence of PFs at both junctions and is confirmed by direct visualization (Figure 6B). The presence of A-C linker in incomplete triplets (C122-C123) is a key observation supporting early linkage establishment. The functional inference about reinforcing the barrel structure (C125) is reasonable but not directly tested.

result: Marked structural differences exist between procentriole and core region triplets in Chlamydomonas, including different MIP patterns, A-C linker structures, and the presence of pinhead versus Y-shaped structures, suggesting sequential recruitment of two protein sets controlled by spatial and temporal regulation, a pattern also observed in mammalian centrioles.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47, C126-C133 compare procentriole and core region structures, identifying specific differences (Y-shaped structure vs. pinhead in C127, different A-C linkers in C128, different PF C1 periodicity in C129, different MIP patterns in C130). The inference of sequential protein recruitment with spatial-temporal control (C131) is reasonable given the documented differences. The observation that similar regional differences occur in mammalian centrioles (C132, citing Greenan et al., 2018) supports the generalization to a common theme (C133), though the specific details differ between organisms.

result: The A-C linker contributes to establishing nine-fold symmetry by restricting the angle between neighboring triplets to ~140 degrees, complementing Sas6 oligomerization, as evidenced by cartwheel-less centrioles in Sas6 mutants that can still form with nine-fold symmetry and by in vitro Sas6 assembly showing variable symmetries.
evaluation: Claims C134-C143 propose a model for how the A-C linker contributes to nine-fold symmetry. The structural observation that the A-C linker restricts angles (C141) is supported by the data. However, the functional claims rely heavily on cited studies of Sas6 mutants (C137-C140) rather than direct experimental validation in this work. The model integrating Sas6 oligomerization and A-C linker stabilization (C142) is a reasonable hypothesis but is not directly tested. The claim also serves as a structural role during assembly (C143) is more directly supported by the observation of A-C linkers in incomplete triplets (C122-C123).

result: The twist motion results in functional consequences including positioning the pinhead close to the cartwheel at the proximal end, increasing exposed surface area for component recruitment, matching axoneme doublet angles at the distal end, and potentially contributing to length control through strain on radial spokes that could reach a balance point with their elastic properties.
evaluation: Claims C144-C151 propose multiple functional consequences of the twist motion. The structural observations (angle changes in C144, positioning in C145) are supported by the data. However, the functional inferences about facilitating recruitment (C146), matching axoneme angles (C147), and especially the length control mechanism (C148-C151) are speculative. The length control model involving strain and elasticity (C149-C151) is presented as speculation ('appealing to envision' in C151) without experimental validation. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not demonstrated in this study.

result: The identified assembly intermediates represent snapshots of MT triplet assembly mechanisms that are tightly controlled by structural components (MIPs, MAPs) and regulatory factors (acetyltransferases, glutamylases), with MIP localization at tubule junctions likely modulating assembly kinetics, consistent with prior EM studies showing non-uniform triplet assembly.
evaluation: Claims C152-C164 synthesize the assembly findings with prior work and propose regulatory mechanisms. The identification of intermediates as biologically relevant (C159) is supported by multiple lines of evidence: length variation (C110), MT end morphology (C107), MT stability (C158), and consistent patterns (Figures 5C-D, 6A-B). The proposal that MIPs and other factors control assembly (C160-C161) is reasonable and supported by citations. The inference about MIP localization affecting kinetics (C163) is plausible given the asymmetric distribution (C162). However, the speculation about MIP assembly kinetics (C164) is not directly tested. Overall, the claims are well-supported but some mechanistic details remain to be validated.

result: The procentriole structure demonstrates extensive biological heterogeneity (compositional and conformational) in situ, and cryoET is uniquely suited to reveal such heterogeneity and provide high-resolution insights into biological mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C165-C166 provide a general conclusion about the work and the utility of cryoET. The demonstration of heterogeneity is well-supported by the data: incomplete B- and C-tubules (compositional heterogeneity) and continuous A-C linker twisting (conformational heterogeneity). The advocacy for cryoET (C166) is justified by the successful application in this study, though it is somewhat promotional. These claims appropriately summarize the broader implications of the work.

result: Background claims establishing the importance of centrioles, their structure, functions, biogenesis, conservation across organisms, and the gap in knowledge regarding complete centriole architecture and assembly mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C9-C31 provide background knowledge from the introduction, establishing context for the study. These claims are appropriately cited (C15, C17, C22-C30) or represent established knowledge (C9-C14, C16, C18-C21, C31). The identification of a knowledge gap (C31) appropriately motivates the current work. These are standard introductory claims that set up the rationale for the study.
